problems.where: S1 and S2 outcome lists (missing outcome)
problems.form_value: Not listed. The notes say: 'Appendix D says AI-arm participants produced shorter ideas on average but gives no numbers and names no study (p. 19); this is not listed as an outcome.'
problems.source_says: The paper states as a finding that participants exposed to LLM stimuli wrote shorter ideas on average, and reads it as reduced elaboration (p. 11 adds 'more superficial ideas'). Idea length is scored on the output, construct elaboration ('Detail or length of a single output'), with AI available, so it bears on with_ai. Form-spec rule 7 asks for every such outcome, even with no numbers: direction treatment_lower, statistics_available ['none']. The paragraph starts from the breadth increase, which occurred only in Study 1, so it most likely concerns Study 1, but the study is not named. Minor: no estimate can come from it.
problems.quote: A plausible explanation is that participants exposed to LLM-generated stimuli produced shorter ideas on average, suggesting reduced elaboration under time constraints.
problems.locator: p. 19, Appendix D, Interpretation; p. 11, Section 5.5.3, first paragraph; codebook section 6 (elaboration); form-spec rule 7

problems.form_value: control_arm 'Participant-generated ideas (both arms)'; comparison_type ai_vs_human; notes 'Context only (AI output versus human output); descriptive.'
problems.source_says: The paper sets the stimulus pool beside participant-generated ideas in general, and half of those (the LLM-assisted arm, M = 0.87, SD 0.05, N 59) were written with AI suggestions on screen. The codebook's AI-versus-human context class requires that 'no person receives AI help', so the label 'AI output versus human output' does not hold for this comparator. The clean context contrast, parallel to S1-O8, is the pool (0.77, SD 0.10) against the human-only arm (0.87, SD 0.04, N 58). The numbers and the direction (pool less clustered) are correct.
problems.quote: We also examined the pool of LLM-generated ideas used as stimuli (M = 0.77, SD = 0.10). Although these ideas were less semantically clustered than participant-generated ideas
problems.locator: p. 10, Section 5.5.2; p. 11, Table 7; codebook section 3 (AI versus human output)

problems.form_value: S2-O1 and S2-O2 do not mention the re-analysis that keeps the excluded ideas and participants (recorded only in S2 participants.exclusions). S1-O2 and S2-O2 end with 'Kruskal-Wallis test.' and omit the parametric check.
problems.source_says: Section 5.1 says that re-including the five excluded ideas and three excluded participants leaves both breadth and depth qualitatively unchanged. Sections 4.6.1 and 5.5.1 say parametric tests give similar or the same conclusions for both outcome variables, not breadth only. Form-spec rule 7 asks for robustness variants in measure_detail. Minor: no coded value is wrong, but the records are incomplete.
problems.quote: a posteriori analysis including these observations provides qualitatively unchanged results for both breadth and depth of exploration
problems.locator: p. 9, Section 5.1; p. 8, Section 4.6.1; p. 10, Section 5.5.1; form-spec rule 7

confirmed: S1-O1 and S1-O2 match Table 4 exactly: breadth 2.32 (1.32, 45) vs 1.60 (0.74, 45), d 0.67; depth 1.13 (0.26, 45) vs 1.15 (0.33, 45), d 0.07. The Kruskal-Wallis results also match: chi2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01, significant after Holm-Bonferroni, and chi2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50 (p. 9, Table 4; p. 8, Section 4.6.1).

S2-O1 and S2-O2 match Table 6 exactly: breadth 1.39 (0.70, 59) vs 1.38 (0.67, 58), d 0.01; depth 1.16 (0.48, 59) vs 1.11 (0.35, 58), d 0.12. The tests also match: chi2(1) = 0.00, p = 1.00 and chi2(1) = 0.07, p = 0.79 (p. 11, Table 6; p. 10, Section 5.5.1).

The similarity numbers match. Study 1: human-only 0.81 (0.08) vs AI arm 0.74 (0.13), M difference 0.07, 95% CI [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, d = 0.91. Study 2: 0.87 (0.04) vs 0.87 (0.05), M difference 0.01, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.02], p = 0.09, d = 0.31. Table 7 lists N (ideas) of 45, 45, 59 and 58 (p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 10, Section 5.5.2; p. 11, Table 7).

The pool numbers match. S1-O8: M difference -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], p = 0.00, d = -1.74, and the pool's similarity went from 0.68 to 0.69 after cleaning. S2-O8: pool M = 0.77, SD = 0.10 (p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 7, Section 4.2; p. 10, Section 5.5.2).

All 16 Appendix D values in S1-O4 to O7 and S2-O4 to O7 match the PDF table. Examples: creativity 4.23 (0.37, 45) vs 4.35 (0.44, 45), and 4.86 (0.74, 59) vs 4.52 (0.88, 58); ideas 2.71 (1.90, 45) vs 1.91 (1.40, 45), and 1.61 (1.02, 59) vs 1.52 (0.78, 58) (p. 18, Appendix D, Descriptive statistics).

ai_available_when_produced 'yes' holds for every participant outcome. In both studies the AI suggestions are on the same page as the idea-submission box. No outcome is produced after AI is removed, so no after_ai record is missing (p. 14, Appendix B; p. 8, Section 4.5; p. 9, Section 5.3).

No outcome is self-reported. Breadth is hand-coded by an author and an independent researcher (99 percent agreement within 1 point, ICC 0.97, scores averaged). The only self-report item is the manipulation check, and the form does not code it as an outcome (p. 7, Sections 4.3 and 4.4.1; p. 9, Section 5.3).

Breadth is the number of semantic categories that one person's ideas span, so flexibility and category_count are right. The paper analyzes breadth and depth 'at the participant level'. Depth is ideas divided by breadth, which no codebook construct fits, so 'other' is right (p. 7, Section 4.4.1; p. 8, Sections 4.4.2 and 4.6.1; p. 10, Section 5.5.1).

The diversity outcomes compare different people. Study 1 keeps only each participant's first idea and then takes all pairs within each condition. In Study 2, N (ideas) is 59 and 58, which equals the participant count (out of 183 ideas), so the first-idea rule holds there too. With AI available, across_people follows the codebook rule (p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 9, Section 5.5; p. 11, Table 7).

Unit 'pair' is supported: 'pairwise cosine similarity scores were computed' and averaged within each condition. Table 7 counts ideas, and the paper does not say what its SDs are computed over, as the form notes (p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 11, Table 7).

The form is right to treat the similarity SD basis as unstated. The d values in Tables 4 and 6 follow from the pooled printed SDs (0.72/1.07 = 0.67). The similarity d of 0.91 cannot come from the printed SDs (0.07/0.108 is about 0.65), so later standardization should not treat it as a pooled-SD effect (p. 9, Table 4; p. 8, Section 4.6.2; p. 11, Table 7).

For the expert ratings, at least two judges rated each idea. Their scores were averaged into an idea score, then averaged across each participant's ideas. N per arm equals the participant count (45/45 and 59/58), so expert_raters and unit participant hold. The constructs are overall_creativity (mean of novelty and usefulness), novelty and usefulness (p. 18, Appendix D).

Number of ideas is a count per participant, so fluency, category_count and unit participant hold. Totals: 208 ideas (2.3 per participant) and 183 (1.56 per participant) (p. 8, Section 4.6; p. 9, Section 5.5; p. 18, Appendix D).

S1-O8's direction (pool more diverse) is supported by Fig. 1: 'Ideas generated by the fine-tuned LLM are more semantically diverse than ideas generated by humans in the control group'. The sign of -0.10 runs opposite to the +0.07 convention (human-only minus AI arm) one sentence earlier (p. 10, Fig. 1; p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

For S1-O8, question 'none', comparison_type ai_vs_human and AI availability 'mixed' are allowed values and fit the form-spec example of AI output compared with human output. The human-only arm had no AI help (form-spec field note on question; p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

The directions match the printed results: Study 1 breadth treatment_higher (p = 0.01); depth, and Study 2 breadth, no_clear_difference; Study 1 similarity lower in the AI arm (more diverse, sign reversed and stated); Study 2 similarity no_clear_difference (p = 0.09). The Appendix D directions follow the sign of the means, and each record says no test was reported (pp. 8-11, 18).

The locators are correct: the end of Section 4.2, and Sections 4.3 and 4.4.1, on p. 7; Sections 4.4.2, 4.5 and 4.6 on p. 8; Table 4 on p. 9; Sections 5.5.1 and 5.5.2 and Fig. 1 on p. 10; Tables 6 and 7 on p. 11; the Appendix D table on p. 18.
summary: Every outcome in the form is scored on the ideas participants wrote (hand-coded categories, embedding similarity of first ideas across people, expert ratings, idea counts), the AI suggestions were on the submission page for all of them, and every reported number, code and locator matches the PDF (Tables 4, 6 and 7; Sections 4.6 and 5.5; Appendix D). The conclusion is refuted only on details: the form leaves out the direction-only finding that AI-exposed participants wrote shorter ideas (elaboration, p. 19), S2-O8 is labeled AI versus human output although half its comparison ideas were written with AI suggestions, and some robustness checks are missing from measure_detail; eligibility under criterion 3 holds.
